title: Antibody-Drug Conjugates: Not Quite Worked Out Yet
body_text: I’ve written several times here over the years about antibody-drug conjugates (most recently here and here), and it’s a field that has seen some ups and downs. Recent years have been more of an upswing, honestly, but I’m starting to wonder if that might be coming to an end. It certainly seems to be doing so over at Pfizer, as reported here at Endpoints. They bought a company specializing in these (Seagen) in 2023 for a cool $43 billion as well as doing other deals in this space, but things have not been going according to plan. In February of last year, they announced that they had dropped Seagen’s felmetatug vedotin. This was an antibody targeting B7-H4, which is a transmembrane protein that’s expressed both on T cells and on several different tumor types (and is tied to poor outcomes in these). It had a protease-cleavable linker attaching it to monomethyl auristatin E, which is the sort of nasty microtuble-targeting payload that ADCs are typically carrying, and the idea was that this one could deliver it selectively into the targeted tumor cells. This one looked very strong in preclinical animal models, but Pfizer said that the data they’d collected made it “unlikely to achieve a meaningful improvement over standard-of-care chemotherapy” in their patient populations. An inlicensed Chinese ADC (disitamab vedotin) (also via Seagen) has been “deprioritized” for HER2-positive bladder cancer patients as well. That one is quite similar to ADC just mentioned (monomethyl auristatin E on a cleavable linker), but this one is of course attached to a HER2-selective antibody. Clinical results here were also not impressive, and Pfizer has an ADC in this space already that they’re continuing with. Then in March of this year, the company dropped the Seagen candidate PF-08046031 for “business reasons”, but I think that translates to “It doesn’t seem to be working well enough for it to ever do any business”. This one targeted CD228, a transferrin protein found on the surface of melanoma cells and several other cancer types, and the phase I trial was aimed at advanced melanoma. They had already stopped work on PF-08046049, which was a bispecific ADC targeting that same protein along with another target, 4-1BB. On top of these, PF-08046045 has been dropped as a lymphoma therapy candidate - it was yet another cleavable-linker-auristatin construct, this one targeting CD30. It was supposed to be an improved version of an existing ADC, Adcetris, but that doesn’t seem to have worked out. And now Pfizer has announced that a late-stage trial in lung cancer for yet another Seagen-derived ADC, sigvotatg vedotin, has failed. There seems to be no difference in survival for patients treated with this one versus standard chemotherapy. This is particularly galling because this was targeting a protein found on the vast majority of non-small-cell lung cancer cells, and the Phase I results looked so good that Pfizer skipped right to Phase III to really get things rolling. But as we demonstrate over and over again, there are no sure things in this business. There are still other clinical trials ongoing with this one (combinations with things like Keytruda) and there are certainly other Seagen ADCs in the clinic for Pfizer or heading there. But all this is illustrating that we still don’t know enough about ADCs in general to pick winners. It’s frustrating - all of these (on paper) look like solid candidates that should hit these tumor types in ways that they have never been hit before. But they keep coming back as no better than old generic chemotherapy drugs - and until we know why that is, we’re going to have to keep crossing our fingers every time another such agent goes into human trials. Will Pfizer every make that $43 billion back?
